newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU set to clear Thomson sale, probes state aid.
newsitem.headline: EU set to clear Thomson sale, probes state aid.

text.p: The European Commission is expected to clear the sale of Thomson-CSF to Lagardere and of Thomson Multimedia SA to Daewoo Electronics Co Ltd, Commission sources said on Monday.
But it is set to attach conditions to 10.8-billion-franc subsidies which France has promised to sweeten the privatisation of the debt-laden defence and consumer electronics group, the sources said.

A decision on the sale of the Thomson SA group is due by Wednesday, a month after the transactions were formally notified for clearance under the European Union's merger rules which ban creation or strenghtening of dominant positions.

Commission officials thought the deal would be cleared without having to go through an in-depth probe because Daewoo currently has virtually no share of the European market. The sale of Thomson-CSF, on the other hand, involved mainly defence aspects which France could, if it wanted, not have submitted to the Commission.
The sale assessment is separate from another EU probe of France's proposed recapitalisation of Thomson by 10.8 billion francs, which falls under European rules governing state aid to businesses.
A decision on this second aspect is expected by December 18, which is when the Commission last meets before its Christmas break.
But some Commission sources said the Commission might try to solve the recapitalisation aspect, at least in principle, before giving its green light to the transactions.
"Were the Commission not to do it, it would be a false authorisation," a source said.

French newspaper Le Monde last weekend published a letter it ssaid was sent by European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert to France's Finance Minister Jean Arthuis which said the recapitalisation plan amounted to state aid.

In return for approving the aid, the Commission apparently demanded in the letter that France submit a restructuring plan for Thomson Multimedia (TMM) that would guarantee the firm's long-term viability, and give the assurance that TMM's share of the consumer electronics market would be frozen for the duration of the plan.
The letter sought a reply by Monday.
Van Miert's spokesman declined to comment on Le Monde's and other French newspaper reports on the issue.
Arthuis, who was in Brussels on Monday to attend an EU meeting, was not expected to meet Van Miert, the spokesman said.
The Commission appears to be particularly eager to know how much of the 10.8-billion-francs package will go to TMM -- which has a worldwide lead in the area of digital television.
